- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Status Workflow

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

36:| R-BUILD-2 | Every record states the firmware image's size in bytes (code, data, bss, the raw image, the stack reserved), from build A. Budgets: R-PERF-1. | M0d | C-FW-SIZE |
106:| R-PERF-1 | Every record states the firmware's code size, static RAM (initialised and zeroed data) and stack high-water mark, and (since M2) its startup instructions and steady-state instructions per period (R-PERF-2), and each stays within the budget `config/budgets.json` sets for the current milestone. Raising a budget, or moving to the next milestone's, takes its own pull request that says why (What/Why/How/Result) and changes nothing else. | M0e | C-PERF, C-UNIT; review (a raise in its own pull request) |
107:| R-PERF-2 | Emulated core-0 instructions are measured in fwtest in two parts (since M2, the owner's decision): from two runs that differ only in length, both ending a quarter of a second past a whole second, the steady state per period (the longer run's instructions less the shorter's, over the periods gained between their ends) and the startup (the shorter run's instructions beyond its periods at the steady-state rate). Each has a budget per milestone in `config/budgets.json` (R-PERF-1). Steady-state instructions per period may also not rise by more than 3% against the latest record of a main commit made under the same steady-state budget, whose own image is re-measured with the same fwtest, runs and options; against a record made under another budget (or none) the change is reported and not gated. Since M3 a record made under the current steady-state budget is a baseline only if its firmware image (SHA-256) differs from that of the last record before the budget was raised: records that still hold the pre-raise image (the raise's own merge, or any merge after it that changed no firmware) are skipped and named in the baseline note, so the order records are written in doesn't matter. (Briefly in M3, before this rule: the first record made under a budget was not compared.) A fall of more than 3% is reported in the record and the pull request's checks. Startup has no 3% gate. No noise allowance: the count is deterministic. Until audio (M4) the period is the heartbeat (one beat per millisecond); from M4 it is the audio block (64 stereo frames, 1.451 ms), counted by fwtest as the rows of `ipb.csv`, and an image with no audio output (one from before M4) has no period, so a baseline made of one is reported, not compared. Until M2 the measure was one one-second run's instructions over its beats, startup included. | M0e, M2, M3, M4 | C-PERF, C-UNIT |
108:| R-PERF-3 | The stack's high-water mark is measured in fwtest: the firmware fills its unused stack with a pattern once at startup (from M1 before any C runs, both stacks; until M1 after the time base started), the stack is captured at the end of the longer perf run (R-PERF-2; until M2 a one-second run), and the lowest word no longer holding the pattern marks the deepest use, including words written as zero. A test build with a known 1 KiB of stack, written with zeros, must read at least 1 024 bytes. | M0e | C-PERF, C-PERF-PROBES, C-UNIT |

Since M2 its columns are unchanged and its instructions and periods are the steady state's (its `period` column says `heartbeat-steady`, and from M4 `audio-block-steady`: the periods are audio blocks); startup is in each record. | M0e | records.yml; C-UNIT |

name: perf-gate-steady-state
description: "Owner's 2026-10-22 decision on how the speed gate treats milestone work (startup vs steady state budgets)"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: d0aa28c2-493e-48cb-b0fd-be2a2d41a714
  modified: 2026-10-22T23:27:49.932Z
---

Decided by the owner in session M2 (2026-10-22): perf measures startup cost and steady-state cost per period separately (two run lengths; steady = difference; record both). Both get per-milestone budgets in config/budgets.json, raised only by their own PR with the reason, like code and RAM. The +3% gate applies only to steady state, between records under the same budget; startup has a budget but no 3% gate. R-PERF-2 amended in its own PR, before the M2 budgets PR.

**Why:** a new milestone's one-off startup work (e.g. M2 drawing the screen) would otherwise fail the +3% gate by design.

**How to apply:** when a milestone adds startup work, raise the startup budget in the budgets PR; keep per-period work within +3% or raise the steady budget in its own PR with the reason.

**M3 rule (owner, 2026-10-23; replaces the first-record rule of #39):** a main record is a speed baseline only if its firmware image SHA-256 differs from the image of the last record before the current steady budget was raised; records still holding that pre-raise image are skipped and named in the baseline note (perf.py choose_baseline). Reason: an unrelated merge (#43) landed between the budgets PR and the firmware PR, and records can be written out of order.

**How to apply:** a milestone raising steady needs only: budgets PR, then firmware PR, in any interleaving with unrelated merges.

**Why:** a new milestone's one-off startup work (e.g. M2 drawing the screen) would otherwise fail the +3% gate by design.

**How to apply:** when a milestone adds startup work, raise the startup budget in the budgets PR; keep per-period work within +3% or raise the steady budget in its own PR with the reason.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
"""Measures the firmware's size, RAM and speed, and gates them (checks
C-PERF and C-PERF-PROBES; R-PERF-1 to R-PERF-5).

  perf.py check --build DIR --out DIR [--base-ref REF] [--records-ref REF]
                [--require-records]
      Measures DIR/app.bin (a tools/build.sh output), finds the latest
      record of a main commit (the first-parent history of --base-ref,
      default origin/main, on --records-ref, default origin/records),
      measures that record's own app.bin the same way, and applies the
      gates. Writes OUT/perf.json. Exit status 1 if a gate failed.
  perf.py probes --build DIR --out DIR
      Builds the firmware with SB_PROBE_SLOW and with SB_PROBE_BIG
      (firmware/src/probe.c), measures each, and checks that the gates
      fail each one for its own reason, measured against DIR/app.bin: the
      slower build its speed and its steady-state budget, the bigger build
      each size budget and its startup budget, with the unmodified build's
      measurements as those budgets. Builds it also with SB_PROBE_STACK
      and checks the stack's high-water mark shows at least the 1 KiB that
      build is known to use.
      Exit status 1 if any gate did not fail as it should.
  perf.py history --record REPORT.json --csv FILE
      Appends the record's line to perf-history.csv (records workflow).
      Never rewrites the file; a commit that already has a line is left.
  perf.py summary --record REPORT.json
      Prints the record's performance as Markdown (for the CI summary).

What is measured (docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, M0e):
- size: code, data, bss, the raw image and the stack reserved, from
  app.size; static RAM is data + bss;
- the stack's high-water mark: the firmware fills its unused stack with
  STACK_FILL once at startup (crt0.S, sb_stack_fill), so the deepest the
  stack went is the lowest word no longer holding it, in the stack
  captured at the end of the run. An image without the fill (an older
  record's) is read by the lowest non-zero word, as fwtest starts RAM at
  zero; that method can't see words written as zero;
- speed (since M2, the owner's decision): emulated core-0 instructions,
  in two parts, from two runs that differ only in length (RUN_MS):
  - steady state, per period: the longer run's instructions less the
    shorter's, divided by the periods gained between their ends. Since M4
    the period is the audio block (64 stereo frames, 1.451 ms), counted by
    fwtest itself as the rows of `ipb.csv` (`--ipb`, which changes no
    count); an image without audio output (one from before M4) has none,
    so its measurement says so and the speed gate doesn't compare with
    it. Until M4 the period was the heartbeat (one beat per millisecond,
    the beats the beacon gained). Both runs end a quarter of a second
    past a whole second, so the window between them holds whole seconds and none of
    the firmware's work timed on whole seconds or tenths of a second
    falls near its ends (an end can come up to about 30 ms late while the
    image idles, docs/HARNESS.md "Time");
  - startup: the instructions of the shorter run beyond its periods at the
    steady-state rate, the one-off work before the firmware settles.
  The stack's high-water mark is read at the end of the longer run.
  Until M2 speed was the instructions of one one-second run divided by
  its beats, startup included.

The gates: each budget in config/budgets.json for the current milestone
must hold: code, static RAM, stack high-water, startup instructions and
steady-state instructions per period. Steady-state instructions per period
may also rise by at most `speed_rise_percent` against the baseline, when
the baseline's record was made under the same steady-state budget;
otherwise that comparison is not made, and the record says why. Since M3
a record under the current budget that still holds the image of the last
record before that budget was raised (the raise's own merge, or any merge
after it that changed no firmware) is never the baseline: it is skipped,
and the baseline note names it (choose_baseline). A fall of
more than that is reported as an improvement. Startup has its budget but
no such comparison. The count is deterministic, so there is no noise
allowance. The baseline is re-measured with this checkout's fwtest, runs
and options, so a change of fwtest or of the method never shows up as a
change of the firmware.

perf-history.csv keeps its columns: since M2 its `instructions`,
`periods` and `instructions_per_period` are the steady state's window,
and its `period` says `heartbeat-steady` (since M4 `audio-block-steady`).
Startup is in each record.
"""
import argparse
import csv
import hashlib
import io
import json
import os
import shutil
import struct
import subprocess
import sys
from fractions import Fraction

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
BUDGETS = os.path.join(ROOT, "config", "budgets.json")
REPO = ROOT                  # where find_baseline looks (tests change it)

# Since M4 the period is the audio block (R-PERF-2): the blocks are
# counted by fwtest itself, as the rows of ipb.csv.
PERIOD = "audio-block-steady"
RUN_MS = (1250, 2250)        # the two runs, shorter first (see the docstring)
BEACON = 0x01C00000          # firmware/app.ld, firmware/src/sb.h
BEACON_LEN = 0x60            # the whole beacon since M2 (firmware/src/sb.h)
# Beacon words (by index) holding the screen's timings since M2, in time
# base ticks (24 a microsecond); an image that doesn't record one leaves 0.
SCREEN_TIMES = (("frame_update_us", 18), ("render_us", 19), ("heartbeat_update_us", 20))
TICKS_PER_US = 24
MARKER = 0x44304253          # "SB0D"
STACK_FILL = 0x4B415453      # "STAK", firmware/src/crt0.S
STACK_TOP = 0x01C7FC00       # firmware/app.ld asserts it
BUDGETED = ("code", "static_ram", "stack_high_water", "startup_instructions", "steady_per_period")
# What the record shows, in order (here and tools/record.py).
MEASURES = ("code", "data", "bss", "image", "static_ram", "stack_reserved", "stack_high_water",
            "stack_method", "startup_instructions", "instructions", "periods", "instructions_per_period",
            "frame_update_us", "render_us", "heartbeat_update_us")
UNIT = {"code": "bytes", "static_ram": "bytes", "stack_high_water": "bytes",
        "startup_instructions": "instructions", "steady_per_period": "instructions per period"}
SIZES = ("code", "data", "bss", "image", "stack")

HISTORY_FIELDS = ["commit", "record_utc", "overall", "milestone", "period",
                  "instructions", "periods", "instructions_per_period",
                  "speed_change_percent", "code", "data", "bss", "image",
                  "static_ram", "stack_reserved", "stack_high_water", "fwtest_image"]


def options(stack, ms=RUN_MS[-1]):
    """A perf run's fwtest options: the instrument. Kept fixed and minimal
    (no watchdog, no captures but these two), because captures change when
    a waiting core 0 is looked at, and with it the count."""
    return ["--ms", str(ms), "--ipb",
            "--ram", "0x%08x:0x%x@end" % (BEACON, BEACON_LEN),
            "--ram", "0x%08x:0x%x@end" % (STACK_TOP - stack, stack)]


def capture_name(addr, length):
    return "ram-%08x-%x-end.bin" % (addr, length)


def read_size(text):
    size = {}
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if line.strip():
            k, v = line.split()
            size[k] = int(v)
    missing = [k for k in SIZES if k not in size]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError("app.size lacks %s" % ", ".join(missing))
    return size


def stack_high_water(data, irq_stack=0):
    """(bytes of stack ever used, the method). With the fill pattern at the
    stack's limit: from the lowest word not holding it to the top. Without
    (an image that doesn't fill): from the lowest non-zero word, which
    misses words written as zero. With irq_stack (app.size's, from M1 on),
    the area's lowest irq_stack bytes are the interrupt stack and the rest
    main's: each is measured from its own limit to its own top, and the
    two are added, since both can be at their deepest at once."""
    if irq_stack and len(data) > irq_stack:
        irq, irq_how = stack_high_water(data[:irq_stack])
        main, main_how = stack_high_water(data[irq_stack:])
        return irq + main, "%s, two stacks" % (main_how if main_how == irq_how else
                                                "%s and %s" % (main_how, irq_how))
    words = struct.unpack("<%dI" % (len(data) // 4), data[:len(data) // 4 * 4])
    if words and words[0] == STACK_FILL:
        for i, w in enumerate(words):
            if w != STACK_FILL:
                return (len(words) - i) * 4, "pattern"
        return 0, "pattern"
    for i, w in enumerate(words):
        if w:
            return (len(words) - i) * 4, "non-zero"
    return 0, "non-zero"


def run_fwtest(image_bytes, size, out, label):
    """Runs the perf runs on an image and returns its measurement: sizes,
    the stack and the last run's outcome from the longer run, speed from
    the two together (steady), the shorter run's instructions beyond its
    beats at that rate (startup), and each run's own numbers in `runs`."""
    runs = [run_once(image_bytes, size, os.path.join(out, "%dms" % ms), label, ms) for ms in RUN_MS]
    m = dict(runs[-1])
    m["runs"] = [{k: r.get(k) for k in ("ms", "outcome", "emulated_ms", "instructions", "periods", "error")
                  if r.get(k) is not None} for r in runs]
    m["options"] = [r["options"] for r in runs]
    bad = [r for r in runs if r.get("error")]
    if bad:
        m["error"] = "the %d ms run: %s" % (bad[0]["ms"], bad[0]["error"])
        m.pop("instructions_per_period", None)
        return m
    short, long_ = runs[0], runs[-1]
    di, dp = long_["instructions"] - short["instructions"], long_["periods"] - short["periods"]
    if dp <= 0 or di < 0:
        m["error"] = "the longer run gained %d audio blocks and %d instructions over the shorter" % (dp, di)
        m.pop("instructions_per_period", None)
        return m
    steady = Fraction(di, dp)
    m.update({"instructions": di, "periods": dp, "instructions_per_period": round(float(steady), 3),
              "startup_instructions": int(round(short["instructions"] - steady * short["periods"]))})
    return m


def run_once(image_bytes, size, out, label, ms):
    """One perf run of ms emulated milliseconds."""
    # tools/fwtest takes inputs from inside the working folder only.
    work = os.path.join(ROOT, "out", "perf-run")
    os.makedirs(work, exist_ok=True)
    img = os.path.join(work, label + ".bin")
    with open(img, "wb") as f:
        f.write(image_bytes)
    opts = options(size["stack"], ms)
    p = subprocess.run(["sh", "tools/fwtest", "run", os.path.relpath(img, ROOT), "--out", out] + opts,
                       cwd=ROOT, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
    log = p.stdout.decode("utf-8", "replace")
    m = {"label": label, "ms": ms, "fwtest_exit": p.returncode, "options": opts}
    return read_run(out, size, m, log)


def read_run(out, size, m, log=""):
    """A perf run's measurement from its outputs in out (run_once): sizes,
    the beacon's marker and beats, the stack, and since M4 the audio
    blocks fwtest finished (the rows of ipb.csv) as its periods."""
    for k in SIZES:
        m[k] = size[k]
    m["stack_reserved"] = size["stack"]
    m["static_ram"] = size["data"] + size["bss"]
    try:
        with open(os.path.join(out, "result.json")) as f:
            result = json.load(f)
        with open(os.path.join(out, capture_name(BEACON, BEACON_LEN)), "rb") as f:
            beacon = f.read()
        with open(os.path.join(out, capture_name(STACK_TOP - size["stack"], size["stack"])), "rb") as f:
            stack = f.read()
    except (OSError, ValueError) as e:
        m["error"] = "fwtest gave no result (%s): %s" % (e, log.strip()[-400:])
        return m
    run = result.get("run", {})
    marker, beats = struct.unpack("<2I", beacon[:8])
    try:
        with open(os.path.join(out, "ipb.csv")) as f:
            blocks = max(0, sum(1 for line in f if line.strip()) - 1)
    except OSError:
        blocks = 0
    words = struct.unpack("<%dI" % (len(beacon) // 4), beacon[:len(beacon) // 4 * 4])
    for k, i in SCREEN_TIMES:
        if i < len(words) and words[i]:
            m[k] = round(words[i] / TICKS_PER_US, 3)
    m.update({"outcome": run.get("outcome"), "emulated_ms": run.get("emulated_ms"),
              "instructions": run.get("instructions", {}).get("core0"),
              "periods": blocks, "beats": beats, "marker": "0x%08x" % marker,
              "stack_high_water": stack_high_water(stack, size.get("irq_stack", 0))[0],
              "stack_method": stack_high_water(stack, size.get("irq_stack", 0))[1]})
    try:
        with open(os.path.join(out, "runner.txt")) as f:
            m["fwtest_image"] = f.readline().split(":", 1)[1].strip()
    except (OSError, IndexError):
        m["fwtest_image"] = ""
    if run.get("outcome") != "completed" or marker != MARKER or not beats or m["instructions"] is None:
        m["error"] = "the perf run did not complete with the marker and a heartbeat " \
                     "(outcome %s, marker 0x%08x, beats %d)" % (run.get("outcome"), marker, beats)
    elif not blocks:
        # An image from before M4 (an older record's) plays no audio, so

UNIT = {"code": "bytes", "static_ram": "bytes", "stack_high_water": "bytes",
        "startup_instructions": "instructions", "steady_per_period": "instructions per period"}
SIZES = ("code", "data", "bss", "image", "stack")

HISTORY_FIELDS = ["commit", "record_utc", "overall", "milestone", "period",
                  "instructions", "periods", "instructions_per_period",
                  "speed_change_percent", "code", "data", "bss", "image",
                  "static_ram", "stack_reserved", "stack_high_water", "fwtest_image"]


def options(stack, ms=RUN_MS[-1]):
    """A perf run's fwtest options: the instrument. Kept fixed and minimal
    (no watchdog, no captures but these two), because captures change when
    a waiting core 0 is looked at, and with it the count."""
    return ["--ms", str(ms), "--ipb",
            "--ram", "0x%08x:0x%x@end" % (BEACON, BEACON_LEN),
            "--ram", "0x%08x:0x%x@end" % (STACK_TOP - stack, stack)]


def capture_name(addr, length):
    return "ram-%08x-%x-end.bin" % (addr, length)


def read_size(text):
    size = {}
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if line.strip():
            k, v = line.split()
            size[k] = int(v)
    missing = [k for k in SIZES if k not in size]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError("app.size lacks %s" % ", ".join(missing))
    return size


def stack_high_water(data, irq_stack=0):
    """(bytes of stack ever used, the method). With the fill pattern at the
    stack's limit: from the lowest word not holding it to the top. Without
    (an image that doesn't fill): from the lowest non-zero word, which
    misses words written as zero. With irq_stack (app.size's, from M1 on),
    the area's lowest irq_stack bytes are the interrupt stack and the rest
    main's: each is measured from its own limit to its own top, and the
    two are added, since both can be at their deepest at once."""
    if irq_stack and len(data) > irq_stack:
        irq, irq_how = stack_high_water(data[:irq_stack])
        main, main_how = stack_high_water(data[irq_stack:])
        return irq + main, "%s, two stacks" % (main_how if main_how == irq_how else
                                                "%s and %s" % (main_how, irq_how))
    words = struct.unpack("<%dI" % (len(data) // 4), data[:len(data) // 4 * 4])
    if words and words[0] == STACK_FILL:
        for i, w in enumerate(words):
            if w != STACK_FILL:
                return (len(words) - i) * 4, "pattern"
        return 0, "pattern"
    for i, w in enumerate(words):
        if w:
            return (len(words) - i) * 4, "non-zero"
    return 0, "non-zero"


def run_fwtest(image_bytes, size, out, label):
    """Runs the perf runs on an image and returns its measurement: sizes,
    the stack and the last run's outcome from the longer run, speed from
    the two together (steady), the shorter run's instructions beyond its
    beats at that rate (startup), and each run's own numbers in `runs`."""
    runs = [run_once(image_bytes, size, os.path.join(out, "%dms" % ms), label, ms) for ms in RUN_MS]
    m = dict(runs[-1])
    m["runs"] = [{k: r.get(k) for k in ("ms", "outcome", "emulated_ms", "instructions", "periods", "error")
                  if r.get(k) is not None} for r in runs]
    m["options"] = [r["options"] for r in runs]
    bad = [r for r in runs if r.get("error")]
    if bad:
        m["error"] = "the %d ms run: %s" % (bad[0]["ms"], bad[0]["error"])
        m.pop("instructions_per_period", None)
        return m
    short, long_ = runs[0], runs[-1]
    di, dp = long_["instructions"] - short["instructions"], long_["periods"] - short["periods"]
    if dp <= 0 or di < 0:
        m["error"] = "the longer run gained %d audio blocks and %d instructions over the shorter" % (dp, di)
        m.pop("instructions_per_period", None)
        return m
    steady = Fraction(di, dp)
    m.update({"instructions": di, "periods": dp, "instructions_per_period": round(float(steady), 3),
              "startup_instructions": int(round(short["instructions"] - steady * short["periods"]))})
    return m


def run_once(image_bytes, size, out, label, ms):
    """One perf run of ms emulated milliseconds."""
    # tools/fwtest takes inputs from inside the working folder only.
    work = os.path.join(ROOT, "out", "perf-run")
    os.makedirs(work, exist_ok=True)
    img = os.path.join(work, label + ".bin")
    with open(img, "wb") as f:
        f.write(image_bytes)
    opts = options(size["stack"], ms)
    p = subprocess.run(["sh", "tools/fwtest", "run", os.path.relpath(img, ROOT), "--out", out] + opts,
                       cwd=ROOT, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
    log = p.stdout.decode("utf-8", "replace")
    m = {"label": label, "ms": ms, "fwtest_exit": p.returncode, "options": opts}
    return read_run(out, size, m, log)


def read_run(out, size, m, log=""):
    """A perf run's measurement from its outputs in out (run_once): sizes,
    the beacon's marker and beats, the stack, and since M4 the audio
    blocks fwtest finished (the rows of ipb.csv) as its periods."""
    for k in SIZES:
        m[k] = size[k]
    m["stack_reserved"] = size["stack"]
    m["static_ram"] = size["data"] + size["bss"]
    try:
        with open(os.path.join(out, "result.json")) as f:
            result = json.load(f)
        with open(os.path.join(out, capture_name(BEACON, BEACON_LEN)), "rb") as f:
            beacon = f.read()
        with open(os.path.join(out, capture_name(STACK_TOP - size["stack"], size["stack"])), "rb") as f:
            stack = f.read()
    except (OSError, ValueError) as e:
        m["error"] = "fwtest gave no result (%s): %s" % (e, log.strip()[-400:])
        return m
    run = result.get("run", {})
    marker, beats = struct.unpack("<2I", beacon[:8])
    try:
        with open(os.path.join(out, "ipb.csv")) as f:
            blocks = max(0, sum(1 for line in f if line.strip()) - 1)
    except OSError:
        blocks = 0
    words = struct.unpack("<%dI" % (len(beacon) // 4), beacon[:len(beacon) // 4 * 4])
    for k, i in SCREEN_TIMES:
        if i < len(words) and words[i]:
            m[k] = round(words[i] / TICKS_PER_US, 3)
    m.update({"outcome": run.get("outcome"), "emulated_ms": run.get("emulated_ms"),
              "instructions": run.get("instructions", {}).get("core0"),
              "periods": blocks, "beats": beats, "marker": "0x%08x" % marker,
              "stack_high_water": stack_high_water(stack, size.get("irq_stack", 0))[0],
              "stack_method": stack_high_water(stack, size.get("irq_stack", 0))[1]})
    try:

            m["fwtest_image"] = f.readline().split(":", 1)[1].strip()
    except (OSError, IndexError):
        m["fwtest_image"] = ""
    if run.get("outcome") != "completed" or marker != MARKER or not beats or m["instructions"] is None:
        m["error"] = "the perf run did not complete with the marker and a heartbeat " \

# fwtest: the harness, as a black box

`fwtest` runs a raw image on an emulated board for a given number of
emulated milliseconds, feeds it timed inputs, and saves what it did:
memory, the screen, the LEDs, the flash chip, the audio, instruction counts.
It is the firmware side's only window into the emulator, and this page is
its whole manual. It says what fwtest does, not how the emulator does it.
Facts about the chip itself (registers, pins, timings, the panel's layout)
belong in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`; ask for one through docs/SPEC-REQUESTS.md.

fwtest is a model. Where it and `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` disagree, the spec is the
authority on the hardware; report the difference as a spec request.

## Running it

The firmware side runs fwtest only through `tools/fwtest`, which runs the
published container image pinned by digest in `config/fwtest-image`
(R-SEP-3). It needs Docker; the image runs as linux/amd64 on any host.

```sh
tools/fwtest run out/build/app.bin --ms 100 --out out/t1 --ram 0x01c00000:64@end
tools/fwtest suite tests/fw/boot.suite --out out/suite
tools/fwtest version
tools/fwtest --image        # the pinned image reference
```

- Run it from the repository root. The current folder is mounted read-only,
  so every input path (image, script, flash file, golden folder, suite) must
  be inside it. `--out` is created and mounted writable on its own, and must
  be empty or not exist yet.
- The container has no network and runs as your user.
- After a run, `tools/fwtest` adds `runner.txt` to the output folder, naming
  the image it ran and whether it was the pinned one. A test record that
  used fwtest names that image; every record also notes the pinned image in
  its environment.

## The raw image

| Rule | Value |
|------|-------|
| Format | A flat binary: the bytes of the code window, from its first byte. No header, no ELF. |
| Load address | The image's first byte is at `0x02000000`, the start of the code window. Link it there. |
| Entry | Core 0 starts at `0x02000000`: the image's first instruction. |
| Size | 1 byte to 1 032 192 bytes (1 MiB less 16 KiB). |
| The flash chip | 1 MiB. Erased (all `0xFF`) unless `--flash FILE` gives its first bytes. The image is then written into it at offset `0x4000`, as an installed image sits. |
| Past the image | Reads in the code window after the image's last byte show the flash chip: window address `0x02000000 + n` shows chip offset `0x4000 + n`. Changes the image makes to the chip (erase, program) show through the window, also over the image's own bytes. |
| Writes to the window | Ignored (and listed as unmodelled accesses). |
| RAM | 1 MiB at `0x01C00000`, all zero at the start. Other memories, and what the real chip has: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`. |
| Core 0 at the start | User mode. Every register is 0, both stack pointers included (set your own stacks first), except `r0` = `0x01C7FC00`: a 64-byte block of zeros whose first word holds `0x01C7FC40`. |
| Core 1 | Does not run until the image releases it (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md` says how). Then it runs alongside core 0. |

## Time

- Emulated time starts at 0 when the image starts. One instruction of core 0
  takes one cycle; there are 240 000 cycles in an emulated millisecond.
- Everything happens at exact emulated times, and the outputs are
  deterministic (below), but **while core 0 waits, fwtest moves time ahead**,
  so that waiting costs (almost) no instructions and instruction counts
  measure work. The rules for that, and what they do to captures, are
  exact; they follow.

### When fwtest treats core 0 as waiting

Two things, and nothing else, count as waiting:

1. **The wait-for-interrupt instruction**, executed by core 0 while no
   interrupt is pending. Time jumps to one cycle before the next scheduled
   event (below). With nothing scheduled, time doesn't jump.
2. **Polling the free-running timer**: reading its count (HW-13 in
   `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, the 24 MHz time base), outside an interrupt handler
   of core 0, for the third time or more in a row with each read coming
   within 64 cycles (64 instructions of core 0) of the one before. On each
   such read, time jumps ahead by up to 20 µs, and never past one cycle
   before the next scheduled event. The read then returns the count for
   the new time.
   - **Only the spacing of the reads matters.** What the loop does between
     them doesn't: stores to RAM, arithmetic, reads of other registers, a
     call. A loop that reads the count every few instructions *and* writes
     a heartbeat to RAM on every pass is waiting, by this rule.
   - A read more than 64 cycles after the previous one starts the count
     again, so a loop whose reads are at least 64 instructions apart is
     never treated as waiting.
   - Reads made while core 0 is in an interrupt handler are ignored: they
     neither count, nor jump, nor break a sequence.
   - Reads by core 1 count in the same sequence as core 0's: the rule
     looks at reads of the count, not at which core made them.
   - Other timers' counters, their pending flags, and RAM flags are not
     part of this rule. Polling them never moves time ahead.

**Scheduled events** are what the emulated chip and the script have coming
next:
- the end of a timer period;
- an audio half-buffer finishing;
- a transfer completing;
- a MIDI byte arriving;
- an encoder contact changing;
- a script event.

They count whether or not their interrupt is enabled. **Captures, the end
of the run and the watchdog are not scheduled events:** a jump never stops
for them.

### What that does to captures

- fwtest looks at the board between runs of core 0 instructions. Each run
  is at most 1024 instructions, and no longer than the instructions that
  would reach the next capture (or the end of the run) at one cycle each.
  Captures, the watchdog, halts and the end of the run are checked only
  between runs. A capture is taken at the first such stop at or after its
  time.
- **While core 0 is busy (not waiting), captures are exact:** taken at the
  first instruction boundary at or after the time asked.
- **While core 0 waits, a capture can come late**, because every jump
  inside a run moves time without using up the run's instructions:
  - Polling the timer: each read can add up to 20 µs. A loop that reads the
    count every *k* instructions can move up to about 1024 / *k* × 20 µs in
    one run, for example 2 ms when *k* is 10. A capture asked for at *t*
    can be taken that much after *t*.
  - Wait-for-interrupt: each wait jumps to the next scheduled event. A run
    that wakes on every event can cross many of them, for example several
    milliseconds of 100 µs interrupts.
- What is late is the moment the capture is taken, not its label. RAM and
  screen captures show the state at the moment fwtest took them, but are
  named for the time asked (`ram-…-10ms.bin`). `leds.csv`'s `ms` column is
  the time asked, while each duty value covers the real time since the
  previous sample. The end of the run, and so every `end` capture, can come
  late in the same way. `result.json`'s `emulated_ms` says when the run
  really ended.
- The watchdog compares its word between runs, so a hang is noticed up to
  one run late.
- None of this varies between runs: the same image, script and options give
  the same late times, byte for byte, everywhere.

### Getting exact timing

- **Don't wait around the times you capture.** Keep core 0 busy then, for
  example by spacing reads of the timer's count at least 64 instructions
  apart, or by waiting on something else: another timer's pending flag, or
  a RAM flag that an interrupt handler sets. Captures are then exact.
- **Or let the image record the time itself.** Store the timer's count (or
  your own tick count) next to what you capture, and check the capture
  against that stored time instead of the time asked. The M0d firmware's
  beacon does this (docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md).
- **For the end of a run**, read `emulated_ms` in `result.json`.
- Instruction counts (`instructions` in `result.json`, `ipb.csv`) do not
  include the time jumped over: a waiting image's counts stay small and
  stable.

### Timers and their acknowledge

The write to a TIMER0 to TIMER3 control register that acknowledges its
interrupt also restarts that timer's count and its period from the moment
of the write. So the time between two of its interrupts is the
period programmed plus the time from the interrupt to the acknowledging
write: about one tick of the 24 MHz time base when the handler acknowledges
first, more when it acknowledges later (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-48). To
measure a period exactly, acknowledge first, or subtract the time the
handler took to reach its acknowledge. Whether the chip does the same is an
open question in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`.

## The LCD

The panel's transfers finish at once: SPI1's done bit always reads 1, and
a DMA transfer of any length up to a whole screen in one `CNT` write
(115 200 bytes) draws (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-29, HW-58). SPI1's `CON`
reads back as last written. A transfer, by DMA or a single byte, that
finishes while `CON` bit 13 is set raises interrupt source 16; with bit 13
clear it raises nothing. A write with bit 14 set acknowledges it, and like
every write it sets the other bits as written: a write of bit 14 alone also
clears bit 13. A transfer that finished with bit 13 set stays pending until
acknowledged, even if bit 13 is cleared afterwards (HW-59).

From fwtest 0.2.0. Before it, a write to `CON` could set bits but never
clear them: once any write had set bit 13, every later transfer raised
source 16, whatever `CON` was written to afterwards (SR-3).

## The command line

```
fwtest run IMAGE --ms MS --out DIR [options]
fwtest suite FILE --out DIR
fwtest version
```

`run` options:

| Option | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `--ms MS` | Run for MS emulated milliseconds (up to three decimals). Required. |
| `--out DIR` | Write the outputs here. Required; must be empty or new. |
| `--script FILE` | Timed inputs (below). |
| `--flash FILE` | The flash chip's first bytes (at most 1 MiB); the rest is erased. |
| `--ram ADDR:LEN@WHEN` | Save LEN bytes of memory at ADDR at WHEN. Numbers in decimal, or hex with `0x`. Only RAM (main RAM and the other RAM banks `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` lists) can be saved; anything else is a usage error. Repeatable. |
| `--lcd WHEN` | Save the screen as a PNG at WHEN. Repeatable. |
| `--leds-every MS` | Sample the LEDs every MS into `leds.csv`. |
| `--flash-out` | Save the whole flash chip at the end (`flash.bin`). |
| `--wav` | Save the audio output (`audio.wav`). |
| `--ipb` | Save instructions per audio block (`ipb.csv`). |
| `--console` | Save the bytes written to the chip's debug message register (`console.txt`; `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` names it). |
| `--watchdog ADDR:MS` | A hang if the 32-bit word at RAM address ADDR stays the same for more than MS ms. |
| `--halt-ok` | A halt counts as success (exit 0). |
| `--golden DIR` | Compare the outputs with the golden files in DIR (below). |

WHEN is a time in ms (`10`, `2.5`) or `end`. The run ends at `--ms`, or
earlier on a fault, halt or hang; `end` captures are taken then.

## Input scripts

A text file, one event per line; `#` starts a comment. Times are emulated
milliseconds with up to three decimals. Events at the same time happen in
the order written.

```
# time   event
2        key 12 down
4        key 12 up

to the panel and to the key matrix.

## Outputs

All in `--out`. A run writes only what it was asked for, plus
`result.json` and `junit.xml`.

| File | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `ram-AAAAAAAA-L-WHEN.bin` | The bytes saved by `--ram` (address as 8 hex digits, length in hex, WHEN as `10ms`, `2.500ms` or `end`). |
| `lcd-WHEN.png` | The screen, 240 x 240, 8-bit RGB, whatever the display's on/off state. Each pixel is the panel's 16-bit colour (5-6-5 bits) with each channel scaled to 8 bits (`c * 255 / 31`, or `/ 63` for green). |

| `flash.bin` | The flash chip (1 MiB) at the end of the run. |
| `audio.wav` | The audio output: 16-bit PCM, stereo, the header says 44 100 Hz. Every sample the output played, in order. How the firmware feeds the output, and its exact rate: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`. |
| `ipb.csv` | Header `block,end_ms,core0,core1`, then one row per audio block (each time the output finished one half of its buffer): its number, the time it finished, and the instructions core 0 and core 1 executed since the previous block (the first row: since the start). Core 0's count is exact; core 1's is counted at a granularity of 1024 core-0 instructions. |
| `console.txt` | The debug console bytes, as written. |
| `result.json` | What happened (below). |

  receiver set up, or more than about a second's worth waiting.

  not model (reads give 0, writes are dropped), with counts, up to 256.

  has something there, ask for it in a spec request.

## Outcomes and exit codes

| Exit | Outcome | When |
|------|---------|------|
| 0 | completed | Ran for `--ms`, and every golden file matched. (Also a halt with `--halt-ok`.) |
| 1 | golden mismatch | A golden file differs (beyond its tolerance), or an output it names is missing. |
| 2 | usage error | Bad arguments, an unreadable or oversized image, a bad script, `--out` not empty, a capture outside RAM. Nothing ran. |
| 3 | fault | A core met an instruction it cannot decode or the emulator does not implement, or its program counter left every memory that can hold code (the image, RAM, the other RAM banks). |
| 4 | halt | Core 0 executed a jump to itself with interrupts disabled: a deliberate stop. The run ends there. |
| 5 | hang | The `--watchdog` word did not change for longer than its time. |

When several apply, the first in this order wins: 2, 3, 5, 1, 4, 0. Captures
and `result.json` are written for 1, 3, 4 and 5 too. Any other exit code
means fwtest itself failed.

### Faults and CPU exceptions

fwtest raises no CPU exception: no condition makes interrupt source 0, 1
or 2 pending, so an image's exception handler is never entered by a fault.
What happens instead (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-52, says it with the measured
values):

- Misaligned loads and stores complete. A word load or store uses the 4
  bytes at the address given; a halfword load from an odd RAM address
  ignores the lowest address bit.
- Reads outside every memory and register fwtest models give 0, writes
  there are dropped, and both are listed in `unmodelled_accesses`; so are
  writes to the code window, which are dropped too.
- A division by zero gives 0.
- An instruction fwtest cannot decode ends the run as a fault (exit 3).
  fwtest may stop at the start of the straight-line code that holds it,
  before any of that code has run, and `result.json` then gives that
  address as the fault's `pc`; to have code run up to it, put the
  instruction behind a call or a branch.
- A jump outside every memory runs what fwtest reads there (zeros) for up to
  1024 instructions, until fwtest next checks the program counter, and then
  ends the run as a fault.

## Golden files

`--golden DIR`: every file in DIR is a golden file, compared with the output
of the same name. A golden file without such an output is a mismatch. Outputs
without a golden file are not compared.

- **Exact by default:** byte for byte. Every fwtest output is deterministic,
  so exact is right unless the firmware's own behaviour is meant to vary.
- **Tolerances**, where an output is meant to be approximate: a text file
  `NAME.tolerance` beside the golden file, one line:
  - `pixel-diff N` (a `.png`): same size; each colour channel of each pixel
    within N.
  - `sample-diff N` (a `.wav`): same format and length; each sample within N.
  - `rel-percent P` (a `.csv`): same lines and fields; text fields equal;
    each integer within P percent of the golden value (at least 1). For
    example `ipb.csv` with `rel-percent 3` is the performance gate R-PERF-2
    will use.
- Golden PNG and WAV files compared with a tolerance must be ones fwtest
  wrote. To make a golden file, run once, check the output by hand, and copy
  it into the golden folder in the same commit as the test.

## Suites

`fwtest suite FILE --out DIR` runs several cases. Each line of FILE:

```
# NAME  EXPECT     IMAGE                 run options (paths relative to FILE)
boot    completed  ../out/build/app.bin  --ms 50 --ram 0x01c00000:16@end --golden golden/boot
stop    halt       images/stop.bin       --ms 10
```

NAME (letters, digits, `-`, `_`) is the case's output folder under DIR.
EXPECT is the outcome expected: `completed`, `halt`, `fault` or `hang`. A
case passes when its outcome is EXPECT and every golden file matches. DIR
also gets `result.json` (every case's result) and `junit.xml` (one test case
per suite case). The exit code is 0 when every case passes, 1 otherwise, 2
on a usage error.

## Determinism

The same image, script, options and fwtest build give byte-identical outputs
on every run and every machine: no host time, no randomness that isn't
seeded the same way every run, nothing from the environment, no host paths
in the results. CI runs the harness's own suite twice in fresh containers
and compares every output byte (C-HARNESS-DET). If two runs of yours ever
differ, that is a bug in fwtest: report it.

## Versions

`fwtest version` prints fwtest's version and the emulator build it carries;
`result.json` has both. The image is identified by its digest. When the
harness changes, a pull request moves `config/fwtest-image` to the new
digest, so a firmware test always names the exact runner it used.

- 0.2.0: SPI1's `CON` writes set and clear bits as written ("The LCD").
- 0.1.0: the first published image.

# fwtest: the harness, as a black box

`fwtest` runs a raw image on an emulated board for a given number of
emulated milliseconds, feeds it timed inputs, and saves what it did:
memory, the screen, the LEDs, the flash chip, the audio, instruction counts.
It is the firmware side's only window into the emulator, and this page is
its whole manual. It says what fwtest does, not how the emulator does it.
Facts about the chip itself (registers, pins, timings, the panel's layout)
belong in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`; ask for one through docs/SPEC-REQUESTS.md.

fwtest is a model. Where it and `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` disagree, the spec is the
authority on the hardware; report the difference as a spec request.

## Running it

The firmware side runs fwtest only through `tools/fwtest`, which runs the
published container image pinned by digest in `config/fwtest-image`
(R-SEP-3). It needs Docker; the image runs as linux/amd64 on any host.

```sh
tools/fwtest run out/build/app.bin --ms 100 --out out/t1 --ram 0x01c00000:64@end
tools/fwtest suite tests/fw/boot.suite --out out/suite
tools/fwtest version
tools/fwtest --image        # the pinned image reference
```

- Run it from the repository root. The current folder is mounted read-only,
  so every input path (image, script, flash file, golden folder, suite) must
  be inside it. `--out` is created and mounted writable on its own, and must
  be empty or not exist yet.
- The container has no network and runs as your user.
- After a run, `tools/fwtest` adds `runner.txt` to the output folder, naming
  the image it ran and whether it was the pinned one. A test record that
  used fwtest names that image; every record also notes the pinned image in
  its environment.

## The raw image

| Rule | Value |
|------|-------|
| Format | A flat binary: the bytes of the code window, from its first byte. No header, no ELF. |
| Load address | The image's first byte is at `0x02000000`, the start of the code window. Link it there. |
| Entry | Core 0 starts at `0x02000000`: the image's first instruction. |
| Size | 1 byte to 1 032 192 bytes (1 MiB less 16 KiB). |
| The flash chip | 1 MiB. Erased (all `0xFF`) unless `--flash FILE` gives its first bytes. The image is then written into it at offset `0x4000`, as an installed image sits. |
| Past the image | Reads in the code window after the image's last byte show the flash chip: window address `0x02000000 + n` shows chip offset `0x4000 + n`. Changes the image makes to the chip (erase, program) show through the window, also over the image's own bytes. |
| Writes to the window | Ignored (and listed as unmodelled accesses). |
| RAM | 1 MiB at `0x01C00000`, all zero at the start. Other memories, and what the real chip has: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`. |
| Core 0 at the start | User mode. Every register is 0, both stack pointers included (set your own stacks first), except `r0` = `0x01C7FC00`: a 64-byte block of zeros whose first word holds `0x01C7FC40`. |
| Core 1 | Does not run until the image releases it (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md` says how). Then it runs alongside core 0. |

## Time

- Emulated time starts at 0 when the image starts. One instruction of core 0
  takes one cycle; there are 240 000 cycles in an emulated millisecond.
- Everything happens at exact emulated times, and the outputs are
  deterministic (below), but **while core 0 waits, fwtest moves time ahead**,
  so that waiting costs (almost) no instructions and instruction counts
  measure work. The rules for that, and what they do to captures, are
  exact; they follow.

### When fwtest treats core 0 as waiting

Two things, and nothing else, count as waiting:

1. **The wait-for-interrupt instruction**, executed by core 0 while no
   interrupt is pending. Time jumps to one cycle before the next scheduled
   event (below). With nothing scheduled, time doesn't jump.
2. **Polling the free-running timer**: reading its count (HW-13 in
   `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, the 24 MHz time base), outside an interrupt handler
   of core 0, for the third time or more in a row with each read coming
   within 64 cycles (64 instructions of core 0) of the one before. On each
   such read, time jumps ahead by up to 20 µs, and never past one cycle
   before the next scheduled event. The read then returns the count for
   the new time.
   - **Only the spacing of the reads matters.** What the loop does between
     them doesn't: stores to RAM, arithmetic, reads of other registers, a
     call. A loop that reads the count every few instructions *and* writes
     a heartbeat to RAM on every pass is waiting, by this rule.
   - A read more than 64 cycles after the previous one starts the count
     again, so a loop whose reads are at least 64 instructions apart is
     never treated as waiting.
   - Reads made while core 0 is in an interrupt handler are ignored: they
     neither count, nor jump, nor break a sequence.
   - Reads by core 1 count in the same sequence as core 0's: the rule
     looks at reads of the count, not at which core made them.
   - Other timers' counters, their pending flags, and RAM flags are not
     part of this rule. Polling them never moves time ahead.

**Scheduled events** are what the emulated chip and the script have coming
next:
- the end of a timer period;
- an audio half-buffer finishing;
- a transfer completing;
- a MIDI byte arriving;
- an encoder contact changing;
- a script event.

They count whether or not their interrupt is enabled. **Captures, the end
of the run and the watchdog are not scheduled events:** a jump never stops
for them.

### What that does to captures

- fwtest looks at the board between runs of core 0 instructions. Each run
  is at most 1024 instructions, and no longer than the instructions that
  would reach the next capture (or the end of the run) at one cycle each.
  Captures, the watchdog, halts and the end of the run are checked only
  between runs. A capture is taken at the first such stop at or after its
  time.
- **While core 0 is busy (not waiting), captures are exact:** taken at the
  first instruction boundary at or after the time asked.
- **While core 0 waits, a capture can come late**, because every jump
  inside a run moves time without using up the run's instructions:
  - Polling the timer: each read can add up to 20 µs. A loop that reads the
    count every *k* instructions can move up to about 1024 / *k* × 20 µs in
    one run, for example 2 ms when *k* is 10. A capture asked for at *t*
    can be taken that much after *t*.
  - Wait-for-interrupt: each wait jumps to the next scheduled event. A run
    that wakes on every event can cross many of them, for example several
    milliseconds of 100 µs interrupts.
- What is late is the moment the capture is taken, not its label. RAM and
  screen captures show the state at the moment fwtest took them, but are
  named for the time asked (`ram-…-10ms.bin`). `leds.csv`'s `ms` column is
  the time asked, while each duty value covers the real time since the
  previous sample. The end of the run, and so every `end` capture, can come
  late in the same way. `result.json`'s `emulated_ms` says when the run
  really ended.
- The watchdog compares its word between runs, so a hang is noticed up to
  one run late.
- None of this varies between runs: the same image, script and options give
  the same late times, byte for byte, everywhere.

### Getting exact timing

- **Don't wait around the times you capture.** Keep core 0 busy then, for
  example by spacing reads of the timer's count at least 64 instructions
  apart, or by waiting on something else: another timer's pending flag, or
  a RAM flag that an interrupt handler sets. Captures are then exact.
- **Or let the image record the time itself.** Store the timer's count (or
  your own tick count) next to what you capture, and check the capture
  against that stored time instead of the time asked. The M0d firmware's
  beacon does this (docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md).
- **For the end of a run**, read `emulated_ms` in `result.json`.
- Instruction counts (`instructions` in `result.json`, `ipb.csv`) do not
  include the time jumped over: a waiting image's counts stay small and
  stable.

### Timers and their acknowledge

The write to a TIMER0 to TIMER3 control register that acknowledges its
interrupt also restarts that timer's count and its period from the moment
of the write. So the time between two of its interrupts is the
period programmed plus the time from the interrupt to the acknowledging
write: about one tick of the 24 MHz time base when the handler acknowledges
first, more when it acknowledges later (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-48). To
measure a period exactly, acknowledge first, or subtract the time the
handler took to reach its acknowledge. Whether the chip does the same is an
open question in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`.

## The LCD

The panel's transfers finish at once: SPI1's done bit always reads 1, and
a DMA transfer of any length up to a whole screen in one `CNT` write
(115 200 bytes) draws (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-29, HW-58). SPI1's `CON`
reads back as last written. A transfer, by DMA or a single byte, that
finishes while `CON` bit 13 is set raises interrupt source 16; with bit 13
clear it raises nothing. A write with bit 14 set acknowledges it, and like
every write it sets the other bits as written: a write of bit 14 alone also
clears bit 13. A transfer that finished with bit 13 set stays pending until
acknowledged, even if bit 13 is cleared afterwards (HW-59).

From fwtest 0.2.0. Before it, a write to `CON` could set bits but never
clear them: once any write had set bit 13, every later transfer raised
source 16, whatever `CON` was written to afterwards (SR-3).

harness changes, a pull request moves `config/fwtest-image` to the new

- 0.2.0: SPI1's `CON` writes set and clear bits as written ("The LCD").

content.content:
### 2026-10-23 M4: the audio output
- Facts: HW-43 (`JL_ALNK0`'s registers, source 11), HW-44 (the buffer at
  `ADR3`, two halves of `LEN` words, left and right alternating, 24-bit
  signed samples sign-extended), HW-45 (`CON0` bit 11 runs it, a frame
  every 544 ticks of 24 MHz, bit 15 the half playing, `CON2` bit 7 a half
  finished and bit 3 its clear, source 11 per half), HW-46 (fwtest reads a
  half when it finishes), HW-19 and HW-20 (the source, its priority), the
  SDK's `WL82.h` (`JL_ALNK0`'s struct). Q-9 (the chip's codec, bits, clock
  and true rate) is open, so nothing here sets up a clock or a codec.
- **Rate:** 24 MHz / 544 = 44 117.647 Hz, the only rate HW-45 gives.
  fwtest's WAV header says 44 100 Hz; every pitch and every measurement
  uses the true rate (taking 44 100 would put every pitch 0.69 cents off).
- **Block:** 64 stereo frames (`LEN` 128), 1.451 ms: 348 160 cycles of core
  0. The buffer is two blocks, 1 KiB. When half h finishes, the other
  starts playing and the engine refills h, which plays next: a sample
  computed now plays one to two blocks later (1.45 to 2.90 ms), and an
  input event waits at most one block for the next refill, so from an
  event's time stamp to its sound is at most two blocks (measured: 1.6 to
  2.9 ms, R-AUD-6). From a key's contact, add M3's debounce (2.5 to
  4.5 ms): measured 4.8 to 6.8 ms. 32 frames would halve that and double
  the interrupts and their fixed costs; 128 would double it. 64 is
  below the 10 ms a player feels on a keyboard, with the per-block costs
  small against the work.
- **Where the engine runs:** in source 11's handler, at priority 0, the
  lowest. The input scan and SPI1 move to 1 and the tick to 2, so the
  tick still preempts everything (its ±1 µs holds: R-IRQ-1, R-AUD-3), the
  scan keeps its 83.3 µs slots while the engine works, and main's drawing
  (which can take longer than a block) never delays a refill. Considered:
  filling from main's loop (a long panel redraw would make it late); a
  short source-11 handler that raises a software interrupt for the fill
  (HW-23), which buys nothing here, as the handler can be the lowest
  priority itself; the engine above the scan (the scan's slots would
  stretch by a whole block's work).
- **Underruns** (R-AUD-3): at each interrupt the half found free (`CON0`
  bit 15 inverted) must be the one expected (the halves alternate);
  after the engine, `CON2` bit 7 set again means the next half finished
  first, so on the chip the half just refilled began to play before it
  was full. Either counts in the audio record and writes `AUDIO UNDERRUN
  nnnn` (the count, hex) to the debug channel; the next half is refilled
  as usual. A test build late for one block in 64 gives exactly one
  report each. The firmware's longest refill: 1.8 µs at rest, 40 µs with
  every voice, the tone and the heaviest input, of 1 451 µs.
- **The audio record** follows the input record at `0x01C00550` (app.ld
  asserts it), with a marker, the start, blocks, underruns, the refill's
  time and nine words for the engine.
- **Core 1** stays parked (R-BOOT-4): one core does all of it with 97%
  to spare, and M5 decides how to split voices.

### 2026-10-23 M4: the audio API
- `firmware/src/audio.h`, beside `input.h`. An engine is one function,
  `void engine(s32 *out, u32 frames)`, called once a block to write 64
  stereo frames, left then right, straight into the half to be played:
  nothing is copied after it, so the engine costs only its own work. The
  words are the hardware's (24-bit, sign-extended), so the API is what
  HW-44 takes, not a format to convert from.
- Events: the engine reads them with `input_read_audio()`, from inside its
  callback, that is between blocks. The input layer queues each event
  twice, for main and for the engine (64 each), so neither reader can
  starve the other, and main's panel screen and LEDs work as in M3 while
  an engine plays. `input_value()` gives any control's state, and each
  event's time stamp lets a later engine place it within a block.
- Rules for an engine: finish within a block (else an underrun is
  reported), expect the tick and the scan to interrupt it, keep samples
  within ±`AUDIO_FULL`, and never call main-context functions
  (`input_read`, `input_led`, the screen).
- Considered: a block of floats (no FPU here, R-BUILD-1's freestanding
  C), 16-bit samples converted by the layer (a copy and a shift per
  word, and 8 bits lost), an engine that pulls events from main's queue
  (two readers of one queue).

### 2026-10-23 M4: the test instrument
- `firmware/src/synth.c`: an engine to prove the path, not a synth.
- **Oscillators:** a 1 025-word sine table (a full cycle in 1 024 steps,
  24-bit), each step linearly interpolated with 15 bits of a 32-bit phase
  (interpolation error about -106 dB). The table is computed at startup
  from sin's series to x^11 in 2^-29 fixed point, a quarter cycle and
  the rest by symmetry, using the core's 32 x 32 to 64-bit multiply (one
  instruction, in our own disassembly): no table copied from
  anywhere and no maths library. Phase increments: the twelve notes of
  the top octave, round(440 * 2^((n - 69) / 12) / rate * 2^32), computed
  offline in double precision; lower octaves halve them, rounded.
- **Voices:** four, from the 27 keys: KEY1 is F3, KEY8 middle C, KEY27 G5
  (the keys are chromatic from F, HW-36's layout), OCT- and OCT+ shift by
  octaves, two each way. A fifth key takes the quietest releasing voice,
  or the oldest, keeping its phase and level, so it changes pitch without
  a step.
- **Envelope:** linear, 5 ms attack (221 samples) and 20 ms release
  (882), from and to exactly 0: a voice that reaches 0 stops, and the
  output at rest is digital silence.
- **Level:** each voice a quarter of full scale, times MASTER's gain,
  the square of its position (roughly even loudness), full at 1 023,
  ramped over each block so a move doesn't click.
- **Test tone:** PLAY starts and stops 1 kHz at half of full scale
  (-6.02 dBFS), whatever MASTER says, with the same ramps.
- Found on the way: the first table overflowed (x^2 at pi/2 doesn't fit
  in 2^-30 fixed point), which the first capture's pitch showed (684 Hz
  for A4); the series is now in 2^-29. A 20-byte character array
  initialised on the stack made the compiler call `memcpy`, which the
  freestanding build doesn't have; the underrun line is a static array.

### 2026-10-23 M4: how the sound is measured
- `tools/audio_analysis.py`, our own, Python's standard library only (so
  no PROVENANCE entry): `wave` reads fwtest's capture; a four-parameter
  sine fit (amplitude, phase, offset, frequency; Gauss-Newton from a
  zero-crossing guess) gives each tone's frequency and level, and its
  residual gives THD+N. Sample times come from `ipb.csv`'s block ends.
- **Clicks:** a step shows as a second difference about the size of the
  step; a sine of amplitude A and angular step w under a linear ramp of
  R samples shows at most A((2 sin(w/2))^2 + (1 + 2w)/R), plus 4 for the
  capture's rounding. Each start and stop is checked against that bound,
  and a unit test shows an abrupt start or stop of the same notes
  exceeds it, from F1 to G7.
- Results (R-AUD-4 to R-AUD-6): the tone 1 000.000000 Hz (0.00000 cents),
  -6.021 dBFS, THD+N -92.2 dB (the 16-bit capture's own rounding is about
  -92 dB at this level); eight notes from F1 to G7 within 0.0003 cents,
  levels within 0.001 dB of MASTER's law, THD+N -74 to -86 dB; every
  sample 0 at rest.
- The golden WAV (R-AUD-7) is exact, so it moves whenever a change moves
  a note by a block; tests/fw/boot.suite says how to renew it. Records
  keep the suite's audio captures as names and SHA-256 only
  (`fwtest-audio.sha256`), not about a megabyte of WAVs a merge.
- Event to sound is timed against the time base's own start, found from
  the captures: the output began one block before its first block ended,
  `sb_audio.start` ticks after the time base began.

### 2026-10-23 M4: what audio costs, and the measure's new period
- R-PERF-2's period is now the audio block, counted by fwtest (the rows of
  `ipb.csv`), and `perf-history.csv`'s `period` says
  `audio-block-steady`. An image from before M4 has no blocks, so a
  baseline made of one is reported, not compared.
- Steady state, instructions a block (two runs, as tools/perf.py does;
  builds `SB_COST_NO_AUDIO` and `SB_COST_SILENT_ENGINE` leave parts out):
  - M3's tick, scan and LEDs, without audio: about 1 440 (992 a ms);
  - the output path alone (an engine writing silence): 1 742, so about
    300 for the interrupt, the checks and 128 stores;
  - the test instrument at rest: 1 813 (+71: reading events and MASTER);
  - four voices and the tone playing: 9 927, so about 1 640 an
    oscillator a block (25.6 a sample).
- Of core 0's 348 160 cycles a block, the platform (M3's input, the
  output path, the instrument at rest) takes 0.52%; all five oscillators
  2.85%. That leaves about 345 000 cycles a block, 99% of core 0, for
  M5's engine, less main's bursts of drawing; core 1 is untouched. In
  fwtest one instruction is one cycle; on the chip, with code run from
  flash through the cache, it will be more, which M4b's real engine and
  a probe on the chip will show.

import sys

CYCLE = 250          # ms; divides the 1 000 ms window between the perf runs
START, END = 100, 2500
HELD = (14, 21, 28, 33)
head = """# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# perfload (tools/perf.py, R-PERF-2): the loaded measure's fixed input,
# the heaviest steady load the firmware has. From 100 ms: PLAY tapped once
# (the test tone on), four keys held (every voice), and then a pattern
# that repeats every 250 ms, so the window between the perf runs (1 250
# and 2 250 ms) holds four whole repeats, until 2 500 ms (past a late end):
# - each held key in turn released for 10 ms and pressed again (the
#   voice releases, then attacks again, so all four keep sounding);
# - all seven encoders turned 15 detents one way and 15 back (each detent
#   is 8 ms of contact changes, so they never rest), alternate encoders
#   in opposite directions;
# - MASTER swept from 1023 to 0 and back, a step every 5 ms.
# Made by a short script from this description; change both together.
#
# time   event
"""
ev = []
ev.append((START, 0, "key 12 tap 50"))
for k in HELD:
    ev.append((START, 1, "key %d down" % k))
t = START + 10
order = 2
while t < END:
    for j, k in enumerate(HELD):
        ev.append((t + 60 * j, order, "key %d up" % k))
        ev.append((t + 60 * j + 10, order, "key %d down" % k))
    for half in (0, 1):
        for e in range(7):
            sign = "+" if (e + half) % 2 == 0 else "-"
            ev.append((t + 125 * half, order, "enc %d %s15" % (e, sign)))
    for i in range(50):
        v = 1023 - round(1023 * i / 25) if i <= 25 else round(1023 * (i - 25) / 25)
        ev.append((t + 5 * i, order, "pot %d" % v))
    t += CYCLE
ev = [x for x in ev if x[0] < END]
ev.sort(key=lambda x: (x[0], x[1]))
out = head + "".join("%-8d %s\n" % (tm, s) for tm, _, s in ev)
open(sys.argv[1], "w").write(out)

# - each held key in turn released for 10 ms and pressed again (the
#   voice releases, then attacks again, so all four keep sounding);
# - all seven encoders turned 15 detents one way and 15 back (each detent
#   is 8 ms of contact changes, so they never rest), alternate encoders
#   in opposite directions;
# - MASTER swept from 1023 to 0 and back, a step every 5 ms.
# Made by a short script from this description; change both together.

# time   event

for k in HELD:

        ev.append((t + 5 * i, order, "pot %d" % v))
